b201.content:
Jerome’s reply to Helvidius, who claimed that Mary had other children after Jesus.

Jerome shows from Scripture that "firstborn" does not imply later children and that the "brothers of the Lord" were relatives, as the word is used in the Bible. It remains a classic defense of Mary’s perpetual virginity.

b202.content:
Jerome’s short and charming account of St. Paul of Thebes, who fled the persecution of Decius and lived alone in the Egyptian desert for some ninety years.

It tells of St. Anthony’s visit to him, the raven that brought them bread, and the two lions that dug Paul’s grave.

b203.content:
More than a hundred letters of the great translator of the Bible, written to friends, popes, monks, and noble Roman women whom he guided in the study of Scripture.

They range from spiritual direction and advice on raising children to fierce controversy, and they show Jerome’s learning, his temper, and his deep love of Scripture.

b204.content:
Fifteen books in which Augustine first sets out the Church’s faith in the Trinity from Scripture and then seeks some understanding of it.

He finds images of the Trinity in the human soul, in memory, understanding, and will, and in the lover, the beloved, and their love. It is one of the deepest works of Christian theology.

b205.content:
A "handbook" on faith, hope, and love, written at the request of a layman named Laurentius.

Following the Creed for faith and the Our Father for hope, Augustine gives a compact summary of his theology of creation, sin, grace, and the last things.

b206.content:
One hundred twenty-four sermons on the Gospel of John, preached to the ordinary people of Hippo.

Augustine reflects on Christ the Word made flesh, the sacraments flowing from his side, and the love that unites the Church to her Lord. They are among his richest spiritual writings.

b207.content:
Ten Easter-week sermons on the First Letter of John, the letter of love.

Augustine teaches that love is the mark of the true Christian and of the Church, and that love of God and neighbor is the root from which every good act must grow.

b208.content:
Augustine’s commentary on all one hundred fifty Psalms, many of them sermons preached to his people.

He hears in the Psalms the voice of the "whole Christ," head and body: sometimes Christ himself praying, sometimes the Church praying in him. It is the longest of his works.

b209.content:
Written soon after Augustine became a priest, this commentary presents the Sermon on the Mount as the perfect pattern of the Christian life.

He links the Beatitudes to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit and to the seven petitions of the Our Father.

b210.content:
Written at Cassiciacum shortly before his baptism, the Soliloquies are a dialogue between Augustine and his own Reason about how to know God and the soul.

They open with a long and moving prayer and show the young convert’s burning desire for God.

b211.content:
St. Paulinus of Nola asked Augustine whether it helped the dead to be buried near the tomb of a martyr.

Augustine answers that the place of burial matters less than the prayers, Masses, and almsgiving offered for the dead, which truly help those who died in Christ.

b212.content:
Cassian traveled through the deserts of Egypt as a young monk and later recorded twenty-four conversations with the great abbots he met there, on prayer, discernment, chastity, friendship, and perfection.

St. Benedict told his monks to read the Conferences, and they carried the wisdom of the Desert Fathers to the West.

b213.content:
Written for monks in Gaul, the Institutes describe the dress, prayer, and daily life of Egyptian monks.

The second half treats the eight principal vices, from gluttony to pride, and their remedies. This list later became the seven deadly sins.

b214.content:
A short guide to telling true Catholic doctrine from heresy. Vincent teaches that we must hold what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all.

He also explains that doctrine truly develops, but as a child grows into an adult, staying the same in nature while growing in clarity. St. John Henry Newman drew on this idea.

b215.content:
Ninety-six sermons preached by Pope Leo in Rome on the feasts and seasons of the Church year: Christmas, Epiphany, Lent, the Passion, Easter, Pentecost, and the feast of Sts. Peter and Paul.

In clear, majestic Latin they proclaim the mystery of Christ, true God and true man. His Christmas sermon begins, "Our Saviour, dearly-beloved, was born today: let us be glad."

b216.content:
A letter from Pope Leo to Flavian, Patriarch of Constantinople, explaining that Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, each acting in communion with the other.

When it was read at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, the bishops are reported to have cried out, "Peter has spoken through Leo!"

b217.content:
A biography of St. Martin of Tours by a friend who knew him personally, written while Martin was still alive.

It tells how the soldier Martin shared his cloak with a beggar, became a monk and bishop, and tirelessly preached to the countryside of Gaul. It became the model for countless later lives of saints.

b218.content:
A vast commentary on the Book of Job, begun as talks to monks in Constantinople when Gregory was papal ambassador there.

Gregory reads Job historically, allegorically, and morally, and makes it a handbook of the moral and spiritual life. It was one of the most read books of the Middle Ages.

b219.content:
Isidore gathered the knowledge of the ancient world into twenty books, explaining the origins of words and things: grammar, medicine, law, theology, animals, stones, cities, ships, and much more.

It served as the encyclopedia of the Middle Ages and preserved much classical learning for later generations.

b220.content:
Written by the abbot of Mount Sinai, the Ladder describes the spiritual life in thirty steps, from renunciation of the world through obedience, repentance, remembrance of death, and humility, up to the virtues of faith, hope, and love.

It is read in Eastern monasteries every Lent and is one of the most beloved spiritual books of the Christian East.

b221.content:
Four groups of a hundred short sayings on love of God and neighbor, written for a monk named Elpidius.

Maximus teaches that love is born of detachment and that the one who loves God cannot help loving every person. The chapters were later included in the Philokalia.

b222.content:
The third part of John Damascene’s Fount of Knowledge, this is a summary of the teaching of the Greek Fathers on God, creation, Christ, the sacraments, Mary, the saints, and icons.

It was the standard textbook of theology in the East and, translated into Latin, influenced St. Thomas Aquinas and the scholastics.

b223.content:
Three treatises written in defense of holy icons when the Byzantine emperor began to destroy them.

John argues that the invisible God cannot be pictured, but since God became visible in the flesh, we can make images of Christ. "I do not worship matter," he writes, "I worship the Creator of matter, who became matter for my sake."

b224.content:
Palladius spent years among the monks of Egypt and Palestine and later wrote these portraits of the men and women he knew there, dedicated to Lausus, an official at the imperial court.

It includes many holy women, such as Melania the Elder, and is one of the main sources for the history of early monasticism.

b225.content:
A collection of hundreds of short stories and sayings gathered by the monk John Moschus as he traveled among monasteries of Palestine, Egypt, Syria, and Sinai.

It offers a vivid picture of monastic life on the eve of the Persian and Arab invasions, full of humor, kindness, and miracles.

b226.content:
Ninety-five prayers, each titled "Speaking with God from the depths of the heart," written by the Armenian monk Gregory of Narek near the end of his life.

In them the poet confesses his sin and pleads for the mercy of God with extraordinary honesty and hope. Armenians have long kept the book as a source of healing, and Pope Francis declared Gregory a Doctor of the Church in 2015.

b227.content:
Philokalia means "love of the beautiful." This anthology gathers writings of Eastern spiritual masters from the fourth to the fifteenth centuries on watchfulness, purity of heart, and the prayer of the heart.

It is the great textbook of the Jesus Prayer and has deeply influenced Eastern Christians, and many in the West, since its publication.

b228.content:
A wandering Russian pilgrim hears in church St. Paul’s command to "pray constantly" and sets out to learn how. A spiritual father teaches him the Jesus Prayer and gives him the Philokalia.

His simple account of praying the name of Jesus with every breath has introduced countless readers, Eastern and Western, to the prayer of the heart.

b229.content:
An early Christian letter, traditionally but not certainly attributed to St. Barnabas, that reads the Old Testament as pointing to Christ.

It ends with the "Two Ways," the way of light and the way of darkness, a moral teaching also found in the Didache.

b230.content:
The ancient eucharistic liturgy of the Church of Jerusalem, traditionally attributed to St. James, the first bishop of the city.

It is still celebrated on certain days in some Eastern Churches, and its hymn "Let all mortal flesh keep silence" is sung in many languages today.

b231.content:
The eucharistic liturgy celebrated on most days of the year in the Byzantine Churches, Catholic and Orthodox, and named after the great Archbishop of Constantinople.

Its prayers, litanies, and hymns, including the Cherubic Hymn and "We have seen the true Light," have nourished Eastern Christians for more than a thousand years.

b232.content: A beloved Christian romance in which the Indian prince Ioasaph, kept from all knowledge of suffering by his father, is converted by the hermit Barlaam through a series of parables. The story is a Christian retelling of the legend of the Buddha. It was long credited to St. John Damascene, though many scholars now link the Greek version to St. Euthymius of Athos. Barlaam and Ioasaph came to be venerated as saints in both East and West. Translated by G. R. Woodward and H. Mattingly (1914).

b233.content: Three treatises written against the iconoclasts, who were destroying icons in the Byzantine Empire. St. John explains why Christians may honor images: because the invisible God became visible in Christ, his human face can be portrayed, and honor given to an image passes to the one it represents. Translated by Mary H. Allies (1898).

b234.content: A short devotional life of St. Columba (Colmcille), the Irish abbot who founded the monastery of Iona and brought the Gospel to the Picts of Scotland, drawing on the early accounts of his prophecies, miracles, and visions.

b235.content: The letters of the great bishop of Milan, written to emperors, bishops, and friends. They include his firm stand against Emperor Theodosius after the massacre at Thessalonica, his defense of the Church’s basilicas against the Arian empress, and pastoral counsel on Scripture and the Christian life. From the Oxford Library of the Fathers (1881).

b237.content: The works of the great teacher of the catechetical school of Alexandria: the Exhortation to the Heathen, which invites pagans to Christ the true Word; The Instructor, a guide to Christian conduct; and the Stromata, or Miscellanies, on faith and true knowledge. Translated by William Wilson (1867–1869).

b239.content: A short treatise on detachment, recollection, and resting the mind in God alone. It has long been printed under the name of St. Albert the Great, though scholars now think it was written later, probably by the Benedictine John of Kastl around 1400. Translated by a Benedictine of Princethorpe Priory.

b240.content: The questions of the Summa Theologica on religion, devotion, prayer, and the active and contemplative lives, gathered into one book. St. Thomas explains what prayer is, why we pray when God already knows our needs, and why contemplation is the highest human activity. Translated by Hugh Pope, O.P. (1914).

b241.content: Letters dictated by St. Catherine to popes, rulers, soldiers, prisoners, and her spiritual family, burning with love for Christ and the Church and urging Pope Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome. Translated by Vida D. Scudder (1905).

b242.content: The Jesuit martyr’s challenge to the Protestant scholars of England, printed on a secret press and left on the benches of the university church at Oxford on commencement day in 1581. In ten short arguments from Scripture, the Fathers, councils, and history, Campion invites them to a public debate on the Catholic faith. He was captured weeks later and executed at Tyburn.
